title: 12 — Design a Chat System
html:
12 — Design a Chat System

The one idea: chat needs server-initiated delivery, so clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a stateful chat tier; everything else (login, profiles, groups) stays stateless HTTP. Messages go into a key-value store keyed by conversation with a per-conversation sortable message ID, and a sync queue per recipient device handles delivery and offline catch-up.

Step 1 — Scope

  • 1:1 and small group chat (≤ 100 members); 50M DAU.
  • Text only, message ≤ 100,000 characters; push notifications when offline.
  • Online presence indicator; multiple devices per account; store history forever.

Step 2 — High-level design

How does the server push to the client?

Technique How Verdict
Polling Client asks every few seconds Wasteful; mostly empty answers
Long polling Request held open until a message or timeout Better; but reconnect churn, server can't tell disconnects easily, sticky routing needed
WebSocket One bidirectional, persistent connection (upgraded from HTTP, port 80/443) ✅ Efficient both ways

Components

---
title: Chat system — high-level architecture
---
flowchart TB
    C1["Client A"] <-->|WebSocket| CS1["Chat servers<br/>(stateful)"]
    C2["Client B"] <-->|WebSocket| CS2["Chat servers"]
    C1 -->|HTTP| API["API servers (stateless)<br/>login, signup, profile, groups"]
    C1 <-->|WebSocket| PS["Presence servers"]
    SD["Service discovery<br/>(ZooKeeper / etcd)"] --> API
    CS1 --> IDG["Message ID generator"]
    CS1 --> MQ["Message sync queues<br/>(per recipient)"]
    MQ --> CS2
    CS1 --> KV[("KV store<br/>chat history")]
    MQ --> PN["Push notification service"]
    API --> RDB[("Relational DB<br/>users, groups, settings")]
  • Stateless services: login, profile, group management — behind a load balancer as usual.
  • Stateful chat servers: hold connections; a client stays connected to one server while online.
  • Service discovery picks the best chat server for a client at login (by region, load).
  • Third party: push notifications for offline users.

Storage

  • Generic data (users, settings, friends) → relational, with replication.
  • Chat history → KV / wide-column store (Cassandra, HBase — as Discord and Facebook Messenger chose), because: enormous volume (tens of billions of messages/day at scale), only recent messages are hot, but random access for search/jump-to-message still needed, and read:write is ~1:1.

Data model

message        (message_id PK, message_from, message_to, content, created_at)
group_message  (channel_id, message_id, message_from, content, created_at)  PK = (channel_id, message_id)

Message ID must be unique and sortable by time within a conversation. A global Snowflake works (→ chapter 07); a local sequence per conversation is enough and cheaper.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 1:1 message flow

---
title: Chat — one-to-one message flow
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as User A
    participant S1 as Chat server 1
    participant ID as ID generator
    participant Q as Sync queue (B)
    participant KV as KV store
    participant S2 as Chat server 2
    participant B as User B
    A->>S1: send(msg)
    S1->>ID: next id
    S1->>Q: enqueue
    S1->>KV: persist
    alt B online
        Q->>S2: deliver
        S2->>B: push over WebSocket
    else B offline
        Q->>Q: push notification service
    end

3.2 Multiple devices

Each device keeps cur_max_message_id. New messages for a device are those where recipient = me and message_id > cur_max_message_id. Each device syncs independently from the KV store.

3.3 Small-group flow

For ≤ 100 members, copy the message into each member's sync inbox — simple, each client checks one inbox. Doesn't scale to huge groups (use fan-out on read there, like celebrity feeds in chapter 11).

3.4 Presence

  • Login → set online + last_active_at in a KV store.
  • Logout → offline.
  • Disconnects are noisy (tunnels, flaky mobile) → heartbeat: client pings every ~5 s; if no heartbeat for ~30 s → offline. Avoids flicker.
  • Fan-out presence changes via pub/sub channels per friend pair — fine for small friend lists; for large groups fetch presence on demand (when the group is opened).

Step 4 — Wrap-up

  • Media (photos/video): upload to object storage, send a URL in the message; thumbnails; compression.
  • End-to-end encryption: only endpoints hold keys (Signal protocol); server stores ciphertext.
  • Client-side caching of recent messages to cut load time.
  • Error handling: when a chat server dies, service discovery routes clients to a new one; clients reconnect and resync from cur_max_message_id.
  • Retry + queue for message resend guarantees.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • ASP.NET Core SignalR — WebSocket with automatic fallback (SSE, long polling), hubs, groups (Groups.AddToGroupAsync(connectionId, conversationId)), and user targeting (Clients.User(id) routes to all of that user's connections = multi-device).
  • Azure SignalR Service — offloads connection management so the app tier becomes stateless; scales to millions of connections. The Redis backplane is the self-hosted alternative for multi-instance SignalR.
  • Azure Web PubSub — raw WebSocket pub/sub for non-SignalR clients.
  • Chat history: Cosmos DB partitioned by conversationId, sorted by message ID; TTL for ephemeral chats.
  • Presence: Redis keys with TTL refreshed by heartbeat (SET presence:{user} online EX 30).
  • Offline push: Notification Hubs.

Review checklist

  • Why WebSocket over polling/long polling.
  • Stateless vs stateful services separated.
  • Storage choice for history justified (volume, access pattern).
  • Per-conversation sortable message ID.
  • Multi-device sync via cur_max_message_id.
  • Presence with heartbeats, not raw connect/disconnect.
